wa_white_chuck_river_boulders_d_ton.blurb: A small bouldering area in the White Chuck River drainage southeast of Darrington, strung along a forest road off the Mountain Loop Highway. Problems run from V2 up to V8: a few moderates in the V2 to V4 range, then a harder group of V6 and V7 lines and a single V8. Much of the area sits under tree cover, and the walk to the first boulder is brief. Think of it as a side trip from Darrington's granite domes rather than a destination in itself. Rain is frequent on this side of the Cascades, so problems can stay damp for a day or two after a long wet spell.

wa_x_rock.blurb: A compact crag in the Olympic National Forest near Lake Cushman, built around a big boulder-like block crossed by two intersecting cracks, which gives it its name. It sits a short way along the trail, up the slope to the left once you reach the old road grade, with a couple of extra routes on the rock above it. Climbs are a mix of sport and trad, with some top-rope options, and grades run from the low 5.6 and 5.7 range up through 5.10 to a handful of 5.11s. Walls in this part of the lake are short, so expect a quick session rather than a big day.

wa_upper_nw_face.blurb: The upper cliff of the large northwest-side faces of Sheeps Head, in the Whistler Canyon area near Oroville in the Okanogan. Climbing is mostly bolted, with a couple of trad lines, and the grades cover a wide spread: one easy 5.3, a cluster of routes from 5.6 to 5.8, and a single 5.10. The base of the upper wall is reached by scrambling up scree and ledges, including a short fourth-class section, so this is more of an adventure than a roadside crag. Descents include walking off or making single-rope rappels.

wa_sam_hill_2.blurb: A sunny, south-facing crag in Lower Icicle Canyon near Leavenworth, with a blend of trad and bolted routes. Grades run from 5.7 through the 5.10 range, and the 5.10s make up the biggest share, so it suits climbers comfortable with moderate to solid leads. With little shade it can be brutal on hot summer days, which makes it a better pick for cooler weather. It sits above the Fridge Boulder, a short uphill hike from the roadside pullout on Icicle Road, and is a neighbour of Trundle Dome and Ski Tracks Crack.

wa_trundle_dome.blurb: One of the Icicle Canyon crags nearest Leavenworth, sitting directly above the roadside pullout opposite the Fridge Boulder. Routes combine cracks protected by gear with bolted face and slab climbing, and the bolting is a bit spaced, so leaders should be comfortable with some distance between clips. Most lines are 80 to 100 feet, which a single 60 metre rope handles. Grades span 5.9 to 5.11, and the 5.11s outnumber the easier lines. The walk in is about ten minutes, heading uphill past the boulder and then bearing left at the fork.

wa_slumbersome_ridge.blurb: A shady wall in Bob's Area on Mt Washington near North Bend, one of the subalpine crags off the Exit 38 corridor. Most of the routes are bolted, with a single trad crack, and grades run from 5.6 up to 5.11c, with the largest group in the 5.11 range. The rock is decent for the area, but many lines want cleaning and the wall is slower than most of its neighbours to dry out. Crowds are rare. The walk is a few minutes beyond Peannacle Point, finishing up a steep, dirty gully on the left.

wa_quadra_crack_wall.blurb: A small, shaded wall at Tumtum, about thirty miles from Spokane, marked by four obvious parallel cracks. It holds a handful of trad lines and some sport, with grades from 5.6 and 5.7 through a group of 5.8s up to 5.10c. The trad lines finish at a shared bolted anchor beside a large tree. From the parking area, head north and scramble up to the left to reach it.

wa_orange_wall_2.blurb: A mostly bolted wall in the Orange Area of Mt Erie on Fidalgo Island near Anacortes. The wall faces west, so it picks up plenty of afternoon sun and sunset views. Most of the climbs are bolted, with a couple of trad lines, and they sit mainly in the 5.10 range with a few 5.11s and one easy outlier. It sits right of the trail past the Cirque, a short walk down from where that path begins.

_conflicts.wa_x_rock: Stored rock is basalt; the Lake Cushman area page calls the rock there metamorphic and mossy (https://www.mountainproject.com/area/114075500/lake-cushman).
_conflicts.wa_trundle_dome: Stored rock is tonalite; the page describes solid granite (https://wenatcheeoutdoors.org/?p=1530). Stored disciplines include bouldering and a V11 problem; neither page mentions bouldering. Same page gives east to southeast exposure.
